newsitem.title: UK: EBRD mulls big funding for Bulgarian industry.
newsitem.headline: EBRD mulls big funding for Bulgarian industry.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is aiming for potential funding of several hundred million dollars for Bulgaria, the bank's team leader for Bulgaria, Olivier Descamps, said on Sunday.
Descamps told Reuters that the funding would be in the form of loans and equity stakes in a number of industrial projects.
They involved "several hundreds of millions of potential funding by the EBRD".
"The projects would be worth half a billion dollars," Descamps said during the EBRD's annual meeting London.
He did not give a figure for the size of the EBRD's contribution to the projects but said the funding could be extended over the next 12 to 15 months.

"We're pushing to play a key role," he said. One Bulgarian project would be announced at the EBRD meeting on Monday in what he called "a large privatisation (with) a large foreign investor". He declined to name the project.

But the deputy governor of the Bulgarian central bank, Plamen Ilchev, said last Thursday that there was a real chance the EBRD would take part in privatising major Bulgarian chemical and cement plants, either as an additional investor or with medium-term funding for modernising the plants.

Earlier this year the EBRD said there were projects in the pipeline that could result in the bank, set up in 1991 to help post-communist Europe to build market economies, committing between $100 and $200 million once the government signed an agreement with the International Monetary Fund.

Bulgaria agreed a $659 million funding package with the IMF on March 17, which has paved the way for other international groupings to extend extra funding. This included about $400 million from the European Union and the Group of 24 richest countries last week.
International groupings and private investors were wary of investing in Bulgaria due to the slow pace of reform under the former Socialist government of ex-communists which led to an economic crisis.
But that government was swept aside by popular protests in February and the present caretaker government has committed Bulgaria to major reforms including rapid privatisation of industry and banking.
Elections are due on April 19 but the reformist Union of Democratic Forces and its allies are tipped to secure a parliamentary majority.
